transcript.text: My child argues when screen time ends. What small step can I try?

requests.reviewNotes: Coach; useful different action on follow-up, one check-in, no invented facts. Aim 60–120 English words or similarly brief Urdu; no automatic follow-up promise.

reply.acknowledgment: It is completely normal for children to push back when transitioning away from screens.
steps: Give a gentle heads-up five minutes before screen time ends so they can mentally prepare.
Use a visual or auditory timer together so the device signals the end, not you.
Offer a predictable, appealing transition activity right after, like a snack or playing a quick game.
reply.checkIn: How does this approach feel to try for your next transition?

transcript.text: Bedtime is killing me — just an expression! Nobody is hurt or at risk; I am tired of negotiating bedtime.

requests.reviewNotes: Coach; useful different action on follow-up, one check-in, no invented facts. Aim 60–120 English words or similarly brief Urdu; no automatic follow-up promise. No false crisis assertion; interpret time and meaning rather than keywords.

reply.acknowledgment: It sounds like bedtime is a real struggle right now, and that exhausting cycle of nightly negotiations can definitely wear you out.
steps: Establish a simple, consistent visual bedtime routine so expectations are clear without constant talking.
Move bedtime 15 minutes earlier to prevent overtiredness, which often triggers extra resistance.
Give limited choices within boundaries, such as letting them pick between two books.

reply.acknowledgment: Managing screen-time arguments can definitely be frustrating, and it is great that you are looking for practical ways to handle them.
steps: Set clear, consistent daily screen-time limits together with your child so expectations are predictable.

Encourage an engaging offline activity right after screen time ends to help them shift focus.
